rosebank-net-zero-politics.headline: Labour MPs press Burnham to block Rosebank as Badenoch makes net-zero abandonment a test for Tory candidates
rosebank-net-zero-politics.body_md:
Andy Burnham's first test of how far a prime minister can hold a line against his own benches is arriving over an oilfield 80 miles north-west of Shetland. Roughly 100 Labour MPs, among them ministerial aides, have told him not to approve Rosebank. Some are reportedly ready to put that into law. The decision is meant to be taken as a quasi-judicial one, which in theory shields it from exactly this kind of pressure.

## The letter and the process

The Guardian reports that 92 backbenchers and at least four frontbenchers signed a letter urging the prime minister not to back the project. Other outlets put the figure at around 100, counting ministerial aides. The signatories argue that approval would "permanently damage our climate credentials as a party and as a country" and could be a "point of no return" for Labour's standing on the issue. They also dispute the economic case. They call Rosebank "not a serious revenue raising measure", estimating that it would raise less than 0.1 per cent of annual UK tax revenue. Another Labour MP, writing in the Guardian, argued that it would not cut household energy bills, because the oil would be sold to the highest bidder.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero says any decision will go through the quasi-judicial process. That process weighs environmental assessments and the public representations received during regulation. It is not a straight ministerial call. In practice this limits what Burnham can say and do. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is reportedly leaning towards rejection but cannot state a view without prejudging the case. The Western Morning News and other reports suggest that eight cabinet ministers oppose approval, and that Chancellor John Healey is keen on it. These accounts are attributed to unnamed sources and have not been confirmed on the record.

No date has been given for the decision. One company with a stake in the project expects an answer by the end of the year. Fahnbulleh approved the Jackdaw field last month, so the department has already shown it will sign off North Sea projects.

## Legislation as the lever

The sharper threat is procedural. The Times reports that opponents could amend the energy independence bill, which has its second reading next week, to write Labour's ban on new oil and gas licences into statute and extend it to Rosebank. One source told the paper that a one-line amendment could be tabled "very easily". The Telegraph reports that the roughly 80 MPs who back new oil and gas projects would be willing to use the same bill to strip the ban out.

That would turn a planning-style decision into a floor fight. It would also put the government in an awkward position. Ministers have to defend a process that is supposed to be insulated from politics, while their own backbenchers show the insulation is thin. A ruling reached under open parliamentary pressure would be easier to challenge in court. Approving the field against it would be costly inside the party.

Public opinion is less settled than the letter suggests. An Independent-reported poll found 52 per cent in favour of approval and 19 per cent against. Support is far higher, at 73 per cent, among the 35 per cent who think approval would lower their bills. Among everyone else it falls to 41 per cent. Backers stress jobs, particularly in north-east Scotland. Critics point to the recent collapse of the Cop31 climate talks in Turkey as a reason for Britain not to loosen its own commitments.

## Badenoch raises the stakes

The Conservatives are making it harder for Labour to find a middle path. The BBC reports that Kemi Badenoch, who has led the party since November 2024, will require candidates to sign a pledge to scrap net-zero targets. The exact wording, scope and timing of the pledge could not be verified for this article. It builds on a position she has held for some time. As leader she has promised to repeal the Climate Change Act, which made the 2050 target legally binding, and to scrap carbon levies on industry. A candidate pledge turns that into a condition of standing for the party.

The two fights feed each other. A Tory party that treats net zero as a loyalty test gives Labour's pro-drilling wing a ready-made attack on its colleagues and gives Labour's climate wing a reason to say the party's identity is at stake. Polling cited in the coverage of Badenoch's policy found that 37 per cent of 2024 Conservative voters would not consider a party that did not back net zero. That suggests the pledge carries electoral risk for the Tories too.

## What to watch

The energy independence bill's second reading next week will show whether an amendment on Rosebank is tabled and how many Labour MPs sign it. The next marker is Fahnbulleh's ruling, which could come before the end of the year. Whichever way it goes, it will set the precedent for how a government with a restive party handles the next North Sea decision.
rosebank-net-zero-politics.in_one_sentence: About 100 Labour MPs are pressing Burnham to reject Rosebank, possibly via an amendment to the energy independence bill, while Badenoch makes scrapping net zero a Tory candidate test.

zelensky-trump-putin.headline: Zelensky calls Trump-Putin friendship 'strange' in BBC interview
zelensky-trump-putin.body_md:
Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly questioned the closeness of Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin. In an interview published by the BBC, Ukraine's president described the friendship between the American and Russian leaders as "strange". The word is mild, but Kyiv's president is the one using it, and he is talking about the man whose support Ukraine most needs.

The interview was published on 28 November. This account rests on the BBC's headline and summary of it. The fuller transcript was not available, so it does not reproduce Zelensky's remarks beyond that one word.

## A relationship Kyiv cannot ignore

The unease is not new. Zelensky has long had to manage a US president who praises Putin as readily as he presses Kyiv. In an exchange with Trump at a joint appearance earlier in the war, Trump himself conceded that his warm words about the Russian leader "sound a little strange". Zelensky smiled and agreed. In a BBC interview with Jeremy Bowen in February 2026, he said he believed Putin had already started a wider war and had to be stopped. He also has said he does not trust Putin.

The latest remark fits that pattern. It is a public expression of doubt about whether Washington's channel to Moscow works for Ukraine's interests. It stops short of open criticism. Zelensky depends on American weapons, intelligence and diplomatic weight, and he has generally framed disagreements with Trump as differences over method rather than ruptures.

## Diplomacy without a result

The timing matters because peace diplomacy has produced no settlement. Talks involving Washington, Kyiv and Moscow have repeatedly stalled, and the disputes over territory, security guarantees and sequencing that held them up have not been resolved. Without a deal, the personal rapport between the two presidents is one of the few variables Kyiv can comment on, even if it cannot control it.

There are two plausible readings of the remark. The first is that it is a signal of concern: Kyiv fears that a president who feels warmly towards Putin may press Ukraine to accept terms it considers unsafe. The second is that it is positioning. It puts on the record a doubt about Moscow's intentions in front of an international audience, including European governments that are being asked to carry more of the financial burden. The interview text itself would be needed to say which emphasis Zelensky intended.

## What to watch

The next test is whether the White House responds, and whether any new round of talks is scheduled. A firm date for direct negotiations would show whether the "strange" friendship is producing movement or only warm words. Until then, Kyiv will keep describing Washington's conduct in terms that are careful to stay short of an open break.
zelensky-trump-putin.in_one_sentence: Ukraine's president described the Trump-Putin friendship as "strange" in a BBC interview, voicing Kyiv's unease while peace diplomacy remains unresolved.

no10-huw-edwards.headline: Downing Street: 'no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards'
no10-huw-edwards.body_md:
Downing Street has distanced itself from Huw Edwards, the former BBC News presenter convicted of child sex abuse image offences. According to the headline on the BBC's UK coverage, No 10 said it has "no interest in hearing from" him.

The BBC report is the only source for this account. The material available for this article gives no date for the statement, no name for the official who made it, and no wording beyond that phrase. It also doesn't say what prompted the question. An approach from Edwards, an honour, a public intervention or a journalist's query could each produce a brush-off like this, and the available material doesn't say which it was. Without that, the line is a reaction to an event that can't be described here.

## Who Edwards is

For two decades Edwards was among the most recognisable faces on British television. He fronted the BBC's election-night coverage and anchored the News at Ten. He also presented the corporation's coverage of major royal occasions, including the announcement of the Queen's death in 2022.

He pleaded guilty in 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children. The images had been sent to him on WhatsApp. He received a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years. He left the BBC's payroll afterwards. His case became one of the most damaging episodes in the corporation's recent history. It also raised questions about how the BBC handled earlier complaints about his conduct.

## What the statement does and doesn't show

Governments routinely decline to engage with people convicted of serious offences. A short, flat refusal is the standard way to do it, because any warmer wording could be read as tolerance. On that reading, the reported line is consistent with settled practice, and it need not signal a change of policy.

The material gives no sign of a new policy on dealing with convicted public figures. It doesn't say whether the statement answered a specific approach or a general press question. Those are different things. A reply to a direct approach would be a story about what Edwards did. A reply to a press question would be only a government position, stated for the record.

The BBC's original report would settle both points. The wider coverage may also show whether the remark came in an on-the-record briefing or a response to a written query.

## What to watch

The thing to look for is the trigger. If Edwards or his representatives made a public move, whether an intervention, a book, an interview or an approach to ministers, the next step would be a response from them or from the BBC. If the question came from the press without any new action by Edwards, the matter will probably end with this one line.
no10-huw-edwards.in_one_sentence: No 10 has reportedly said it has 'no interest in hearing from' Huw Edwards, the disgraced ex-BBC presenter, but what prompted the remark is not established.

spain-election-final-pitch.headline: Spanish PM and rivals make final pitch ahead of election
spain-election-final-pitch.body_md:
Spain votes on Sunday in a snap general election that the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called after parliament rejected two of his government's housing decrees. The final campaign rallies are over. The last published polls, from 23 and 24 November, put the conservative Popular Party (PP) of Alberto Núñez Feijóo ahead. Whether it can govern depends on a party that has never sat in a Spanish government since the end of the Franco dictatorship.

The result matters beyond Spain's borders. Spain is the euro area's fourth-largest economy, and a durable government in Madrid underpins confidence in its budget and reform plans. That confidence is what holds down borrowing costs across the euro-area periphery. Bond investors are the obvious audience, though neither of the sources used here reported any bond-market data. The piece is therefore framed around the stakes rather than a market reaction.

## How Spain got here

The last general election was in July 2023, and the legal deadline for the next was 2027. Sánchez's minority coalition of the Socialists (PSOE) and the left-wing Sumar alliance never held a stable majority. It relied on EH Bildu, the BNG, the PNV and ERC. Junts, the Catalan party whose votes helped secure his 2023 investiture, has since repeatedly voted against the government.

Housing finished the arrangement. Mass protests over rents and prices preceded the defeat of the government's relief measures in parliament, and the early vote followed. In an October YouGov survey, 53% of respondents named housing as one of the two most important issues. Home prices nearly doubled in the decade to the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat. Analysts cited by Al Jazeera put the shortfall at 750,000 homes.

The two main parties offer opposite remedies. The PP would repeal the 2023 housing law and scrap rent caps in high-pressure areas. The Socialists would extend renter protections and require at least a quarter of new homes to be public or permanently price-restricted.

## The arithmetic

The Congress of Deputies has 350 seats, so a majority needs 176. The final El País average, published on 24 November, had the PP on 31.4%, the Socialists on 29.1% and the far-right Vox on 17.9%. Four polls published a week before the vote, by Ipsos, Data10, GAD3 and Hamalgama Métrica, all put the PP first. They differ on the size of its lead and on Vox's result. Several seat projections place a PP–Vox bloc above 176. At least one aggregator, Election Trend, still shows a result without a clear majority. Spanish law bans publishing new polls in the final five days, so these are the last numbers.

A PP win alone would therefore not settle the question. The PP is expected to win the most seats but to need Vox to reach 176. That would put the far right in a Spanish cabinet for the first time since 1975. Immigration is the likely point of friction in such a coalition, particularly after the Ceuta crossings in July. Vox also campaigns on lower taxes and against Catalan and Basque separatism. Sánchez's route back is narrower. He would need to rebuild the same patchwork of regional and left-wing parties, with Junts a less reliable partner than before and a new Broad Front led by Ada Colau replacing Sumar. Podemos is running separately.

## What the campaign argued about

Feijóo ran on cost of living and corruption, telling a rally in Murcia on 22 November that voters should not forget that "inflation is eating into your pay check". Inflation reached 4.9% in October, against 4% for the euro zone, and a November flash estimate showed it easing to 4.1%. The government also faces criticism over two deadly train collisions and several corruption cases.

Sánchez's pitch leaned on the economy and on foreign policy. Spain grew 2.7% year on year in the third quarter, against 1.3% for the euro zone. He also used the campaign to distance himself from Washington, asking what good President Trump had brought to the United States and the world. Neither main party has committed to NATO's target of spending 5% of GDP on defence, a figure that would strain any budget.

## What to watch

Polls close at 8pm local time on Sunday, and first results are expected that night. The first test is whether the PP and Vox together reach 176 seats. If they do not, Spain may face weeks of negotiation or a repeat of the stalemates it endured in 2019. The second test is the budget. A government that cannot pass spending plans would leave Madrid's fiscal path less predictable. A PP–Vox coalition would instead raise questions about how far tax cuts and defence commitments can be reconciled with deficit targets. Neither outcome is a crisis on current evidence, but the coalition that emerges will decide how that fiscal path reads to investors. Elsewhere in the euro area, France's slide into recession leaves less room for a second large economy to wobble.
spain-election-final-pitch.in_one_sentence: Spain votes on 29 November after Sánchez called a snap election; polls favour the PP but it likely needs far-right Vox for a majority, a coalition question that matters for euro-area fiscal credibility.

huawei-verdict.headline: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
huawei-verdict.body_md:
A federal jury in Brooklyn has convicted Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets from American companies. It has also cleared the company of the racketeering charge that prosecutors had used to tie the whole case together. The verdict, returned on 24 November, leaves the US government with a conviction on most of what it alleged and without the single count that framed it as a criminal enterprise.

## What the jury decided

According to reports of the verdict, the jury convicted Huawei Technologies and three subsidiaries on 10 of 12 counts. The subsidiaries are Huawei Device, Futurewei Technologies and Huawei Device USA. The convictions cover conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering and violations of US sanctions on Iran.

Jurors acquitted on two counts: racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.

The headline needs a qualifier. The trade-secret conviction is one of ten, and the bank-fraud and sanctions convictions sit alongside it. The racketeering acquittal is the largest single loss for prosecutors, but it is not the whole of the verdict.

## Why the racketeering count mattered

Racketeering law, usually called RICO, lets prosecutors treat a series of separate offences as the output of one organisation. That makes it a useful way to present a sprawling case to a jury. Huawei's lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said the racketeering count was "the only count that brought all of the allegations together", and that the jury rejected it.

This reading comes from the defence, so it should be weighed accordingly. Even so, the outcome is consistent with it. Jurors seem to have been willing to convict on specific conduct, such as the sanctions violations and the theft of secrets. They were not willing to find that the conduct amounted to a company-wide criminal enterprise.

That distinction affects how the case can be used. A racketeering conviction would have supported the broader government argument that Huawei's misconduct was systemic. Without it, the convictions stand as findings on particular schemes.

## Huawei's response and what comes next

Huawei called the remaining convictions "equally without legal or factual merit". It said the five trade-secret disputes cited by prosecutors had previously been resolved as civil matters. Heberlig said the company would appeal. Reports put the trial at roughly three months, with accounts differing between about 11 and 12 weeks.

Sentencing is scheduled for September 2027. Until then, the penalties are unknown. A corporation cannot be jailed, so the practical consequences will come through fines, any forfeiture and the knock-on effects for Huawei's dealings with banks and Western partners. None of that has been set. An appeal could take years and may target the trade-secret findings, where the company's argument rests on the earlier civil settlements.

The case is a different matter from a 2019 Texas civil trial, in which a jury cleared CNEX Labs of stealing Huawei's trade secrets. That dispute is unrelated to this prosecution.

The next markers are the post-trial motions and the September 2027 sentencing. Those will show how heavy the penalties are and whether the convictions survive Huawei's challenge.

meta-muse-uk.headline: Meta launches AI shopping agent Muse in the UK
meta-muse-uk.body_md:
Meta is reported to be rolling out an AI shopping assistant called Muse to users in the UK. If it works as described, one of the country's biggest social platforms would sit between shoppers and the retailers they buy from.

The detail available is thin. The report comes from trade outlet Just Style, as relayed in an internal discovery brief. This article has not independently confirmed it. There is no confirmed launch date, no figure for how many people can use Muse, and no list of the retailers involved. Meta's own announcement has not been checked.

## What 'agentic' is meant to mean

Muse is described as an "agentic" assistant. In plain terms, that means it is meant to act for the user, not just answer questions. A chatbot that suggests a pair of trainers is one thing. An agent that finds them, compares prices and moves towards a purchase is another.

The brief does not say which of those steps Muse performs. It is unclear whether it completes payments, whether it buys inside Meta's apps or hands users off to a retailer's site, or whether it draws on products listed on Meta's platforms or on the wider web. Each of those choices changes the commercial picture a great deal, and none has been established.

## Why retailers would care

The brief frames Muse as competing with retailers and marketplaces. That framing has not been checked against a primary source, and "competing" may be stronger than the facts support. An assistant that recommends products from existing retailers is a different thing from one that sells goods itself.

The underlying concern is still easy to follow. Retailers and marketplaces pay for traffic. They bid for ads, pay commissions and optimise their listings so shoppers find them. An assistant that answers "what should I buy?" directly can shrink the number of shoppers who browse a retailer's own site. It can also shift who decides what appears first.

That would matter in three ways:

- **Traffic.** Fewer direct visits would leave retailers more dependent on whichever platform the assistant lives in.
- **Economics.** A platform that originates the sale may expect a cut, or may charge for placement in its recommendations.
- **Control of the decision.** If the assistant ranks and filters options, the shopper sees what it chooses to show. How it makes those choices is the open question.

Meta is not the only company pursuing this. Other large technology firms have been building shopping features into their AI assistants. This article does not verify any specific rival product or launch.

## What is still missing

Several things would turn this from a reported rollout into something firm: a statement from Meta describing Muse's functions and availability; confirmation of which UK retailers or marketplaces participate; and any detail on fees, data use and how product results are ranked. UK regulators have taken an interest in how large platforms steer consumers, so any disclosure on those points would be worth reading closely.

Until Meta or a retailer confirms the details, Muse should be treated as a reported launch with unknown scope. The next useful data point is an official Meta announcement or retailer statement setting out what the assistant can actually do.
meta-muse-uk.in_one_sentence: Meta's agentic shopping assistant Muse is reportedly rolling out to UK users, but its scope, date and effect on retailers remain unconfirmed.

burnham-rough-sleepers.headline: Burnham's Christmas vow: a third of rough sleepers offered a bed or support
burnham-rough-sleepers.body_md:
Ministers say a little over a third of people sleeping rough in England have been offered a bed or support since the prime minister's Christmas pledge on rough sleeping. The government calls this "early progress". The published figures do not show how many people accepted an offer or are still on the street.

Andy Burnham has promised a route off the street for everyone sleeping rough in England by Christmas. The drive is backed by £442m of winter funding, and government material puts the longer-term commitment at £874m over three years for extra bed spaces and expanded outreach. It borrows from Greater Manchester's A Bed Every Night scheme, which Burnham championed as mayor and which now offers about 600 beds a night. Ministers have said the pledge does not mean everyone will have permanent housing by Christmas, only an offer.

## What the figures say

Official figures released on Friday 27 November show that councils made offers to 3,276 people in October, after the funding was distributed on 30 September. Set against an estimate of 9,369 people sleeping rough in September, that is about 35%, which is where the "third" comes from.

The comparison is looser than it looks. The two numbers cover different months and different methods: one counts people offered help, the other is an estimate of people sleeping rough. They do not show what share of those counted in September received help. Some councils were also unable to report how many people they had helped. Reports differ on the total as well. One cites 4,251 offers made so far, while 3,276 is the number of people who received at least one offer.

Ministers also said 497 people were occupying nearly 2,000 new bed spaces. That figure is closer to an outcome measure than the offers count, though it is a small share of the people involved.

## What is not yet known

Campaigners say the government has not disclosed how many offers were declined, and the published data do not show how many people left the streets. That matters because rough sleeping is not a fixed group. People who have been outside for long periods may not accept an offer straight away. Others who are offered a bed return to the street within days.

The homelessness charity Porchlight has warned that a short stay without a lasting home can leave people trapped in the cycle, and Shelter has argued that ending rough sleeping has to include building council homes. Burnham himself has acknowledged that government money alone may not be enough.

Councils are only partly confident. About 63% told the government they expect to meet the target of offering everyone a route off the street by 1 December. 14% said they were not confident, and just over a fifth did not give a view.

## What to watch

The pledge is worded as an offer, so the first test is whether the offers count approaches the true number of people sleeping rough by the 1 December deadline. The harder test is what follows: how many accept, how many are still in accommodation in the new year, and whether the next official rough sleeping snapshot shows a fall. Until the government publishes acceptance and retention figures, "early progress" describes activity rather than results.

slapp-whistleblowers.headline: Government to curb SLAPP claims against whistleblowers; Meta whistleblower urges NDA ban
slapp-whistleblowers.body_md:
The government is preparing to limit the use of SLAPPs, the strategic lawsuits that wealthy people and companies use to frighten critics into silence, against whistleblowers. Meanwhile, a former Meta executive has used a London lecture to press Prime Minister Andy Burnham to go further and restrict the non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) that keep many workers quiet.

The two measures target different tools. A SLAPP is a legal claim, often for defamation or breach of confidence, whose aim is to impose ruinous costs instead of winning in court. An NDA works earlier and more quietly: a worker signs it, often as part of a severance deal, and the threat of legal action does the rest.

## What is known about the SLAPP move

The detail is thin. BBC Politics and the Guardian report that the government will curb SLAPP-style claims aimed at whistleblowers. At the time of writing, no bill name, timetable or definition of the claims covered had been confirmed in the sources reviewed, so how wide the protection will run is not yet clear.

The backdrop is slow progress. Campaigners have pressed for general anti-SLAPP legislation for years, and two private members' bills, one in each House of Parliament, have been introduced. Reports in recent months have said the government has promised its own legislation "as soon as time allows". Any such protection would apply to England and Wales only, because the matter is devolved.

## The case for going further

Sarah Wynn-Williams, Meta's former director of global public policy, made the argument on 27 November at London's annual Orwell lecture. She welcomed Mr Burnham's earlier commitment to restrict NDAs, which is aimed at victims of crime and workplace harassment. She said it does not go far enough.

She made two demands. The first is that any restrictions apply retroactively, to agreements already signed. Without that, she argued, many people would stay muzzled. The second is that the limits reach beyond harassment to cover insiders who know about the risks of artificial intelligence and are contractually barred from saying so. She likened NDAs to the "memory hole" in Orwell's *1984*. She also cited cases involving David Walliams and Russell Brand, where reports suggest NDAs were used to silence women on matters of public concern.

Her own position gives the argument force. She remains restricted by an interim arbitration ruling that Meta obtained over her memoir, *Careless People*. Meta disputes the book's accuracy and has called her legal challenge a commercial scheme.

## Where the government stands

The government's current NDA work is narrower than she wants. A consultation, launched on 15 April and closed on 8 July, asked what conditions an NDA must meet to stay valid, whom workers must be free to speak to, and whether protections should reach agency workers and the self-employed. It covers harassment and discrimination, and changes are expected to take effect in 2027. Employment Rights Minister Kate Dearden said at the launch: "We are committed to ending a culture of silence and impunity." A separate review of the whistleblowing framework was also promised.

That leaves the real question. Limiting SLAPPs would stop employers suing whistleblowers after they speak. A wider NDA ban would stop the silence being bought before anyone speaks, and would reach technology firms where the issue is a safety concern with no harassment or crime involved. Which way the government goes should become clearer when it publishes its response to the NDA consultation and sets out the scope of its SLAPP measure.

spacex-million-satellites.headline: Regulators approve SpaceX plan for a million data satellites
spacex-million-satellites.body_md:
US regulators have approved SpaceX's plan to put up to a million data-processing satellites into orbit. It is the largest satellite licence ever contemplated, and astronomers and environmental groups are already objecting.

The Federal Communications Commission cleared the constellation, which SpaceX calls Starmind, on Wednesday, according to reporting by the BBC and advocacy group accounts. SpaceX filed the application on 30 January. It describes a network of solar-powered satellites that would carry out computing in orbit rather than on the ground, to meet demand from artificial intelligence. Deployment is targeted by 2040.

## What was approved, and what is not yet clear

The headline number needs care. The reports describe approval of a plan for "up to" a million satellites. They do not make clear whether that is a full licence or a staged authorisation, or what conditions attach. The FCC's order was not available to this writer, and the reporting does not set out the terms. Earlier precedent argues for caution: in 2022 the FCC approved 7,500 additional Starlink satellites, well short of the nearly 30,000 SpaceX first requested.

The filing proposed narrow orbital shells, each up to 50km deep, at altitudes of roughly 500km to 2,000km. Nothing public says who would buy the computing, or how SpaceX would deal with heat. Dumping heat is hard in a vacuum, and launch costs and debris are further engineering doubts. FCC chairman Brendan Carr called the plan "a bold new frontier" and said it would take the world into "the era of super intelligence."

## The objections

The sharpest objections come from two groups. The American Astronomical Society said it was "disheartened and dismayed" and that the constellation "would significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities". It warned that radio astronomy in particular was at risk. Optical astronomers have complained for years that existing satellite constellations leave streaks across images. A fleet of this size is a different order of magnitude: there are only some 15,000 working satellites in orbit today.

Environmental groups make a legal argument as well. Earthjustice's Jan Hasselman said that "the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals." Critics say the approval came without the environmental review required under the National Environmental Policy Act. Tim Whitehouse of Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility called it "reckless". A challenge in the courts is plausible, though none has been reported yet.

## What to watch

Three things will show how big this really is. The first is the text of the FCC order: the number of satellites authorised at each stage, any milestones, and any debris or astronomy conditions. The second is whether a legal challenge is filed over the missing environmental review. The third is whether SpaceX starts launching Starmind hardware, and whether any customer for orbital computing emerges. A licence is permission, not a working system, and the distance between a million-satellite filing and a million satellites is very large.

sprouts-hydrogen.headline: Heat and drought hit UK sprouts; BP and Iberdrola open Spain's largest green hydrogen plant
sprouts-hydrogen.body_md:
Two climate stories, one about food on the table and one about fuel for industry, share the same question. Do the effects of a warming climate and the plans to cut emissions show up in the real economy yet? The first is a seasonal story: heat and drought are reported to have cut this year's UK Brussels sprout yields. The second is a hydrogen plant on Spain's Mediterranean coast.

## Sprouts under strain

The Guardian reports that heatwaves and drought have reduced UK sprout yields, which could make the Christmas staple dearer. The Bot Tribune has not been able to confirm the figures behind that account. No yield shortfall, acreage, growing region or retail price change has been independently verified, and the size of any price rise is unknown. Searches turned up no 2026 estimates from the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) or the British Growers Association, and no wholesale price data.

The wider conditions are better documented. One trade report, from FreshPlaza, describes high temperatures and dry weather raising flea beetle pressure on sprouts in Oxfordshire, and says lower yields have already lifted prices of other Christmas crops, potatoes and broccoli among them. The same report cites the Met Office describing summer 2026 as the hottest on record, with drought declared across Wales and much of England. That is a single trade source, and it does not mention sprout prices.

Past seasons offer only limited guidance. Growers in 2018 and 2022 also warned of lighter yields and smaller stalks after hot, dry summers, and supermarkets generally kept sprouts on shelves. Weather stress tends to show up first in crop size, quality and the cost of irrigation and replanting. Shortages and shelf prices are a later and less certain consequence. Households should read the sprout price effect as plausible but not yet measured.

## Hydrogen in Castellón

The second story is about whether a promised technology is actually being built. BP and Iberdrola's 50/50 joint venture, Castellón Green Hydrogen, has a 25 megawatt electrolyser at BP's refinery in Castellón. The companies describe it as Spain's largest green hydrogen project. The investment is more than €70m, helped by about €15m from Spanish recovery-plan programmes. Iberdrola supplies the electricity from its solar and wind farms under a power purchase agreement.

The plant is designed to produce around 2,800 tonnes of green hydrogen a year, which will replace part of the grey hydrogen, made from natural gas, that the refinery now uses. The companies took a final investment decision in 2024 and began construction in early 2025. PV Magazine reported on 1 July 2026 that construction was complete and commissioning tests had begun. The companies have said production should start before the end of the year.

The "largest" label needs context. At 25 MW the plant is large for Spain but small beside the multi-gigawatt projects that have been proposed worldwide. Its significance is that it exists, with refinery demand and a power contract behind it. That is a more demanding test than an announcement. Whether it reaches full, steady output is not yet confirmed.

## What to watch

Two data points will settle most of this. The AHDB and the British Growers Association should publish crop and price figures as Christmas approaches, and those will show whether the sprout shortfall is real and how large it is. For Castellón, the question is whether the companies confirm first hydrogen production before the year ends, and at what output.

gta6-ai-clones.headline: Gamers use AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6
gta6-ai-clones.body_md:
Take-Two Interactive is trying to shut down a wave of fan projects that use leaked files and AI coding tools to run Grand Theft Auto 6 on PCs. The game exists officially only on consoles. The episode shows how little it now takes for hobbyists to try to rebuild a studio's work, and how hard that is to police.

## What happened

Earlier this month a hacker or group calling itself Cyberleek released what it said was a near-complete Xbox development build of GTA 6. It later claimed to have leaked the missing executable file needed to launch it. Rockstar and Take-Two have not confirmed that the build is genuine.

The game has since launched on consoles. One report puts its first full day of retail sales at $3.8bn (£2.9bn), which would make it the biggest entertainment launch on record. Rockstar has not announced a PC version. For comparison, GTA 5 reached PC 19 months after its console release. That gap leaves an obvious opening for fans.

One leak-based effort was called Leonida. Its Discord server had almost 180,000 members when it went offline. Developers there tried to get the leaked Xbox build running on Windows. The project's defenders said users would "bring their own files". Take-Two called that framing "intentionally misleading". Its argument was that the only files anyone could realistically bring were the leaked ones. Its notice called the project a derivative work of GTA VI. GitHub processed the takedown against 3,007 repositories, covering the main project and its forks. One notice said: "There are no remedies available to rectify this clear attempt to facilitate copyright infringement."

## Where AI comes in

There are two different things going on, and they carry different legal weight.

The first is replication. A user asks a chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game that resembles an existing one, working from screenshots or descriptions. That produces a lookalike. It does not copy the original's code or assets.

The second is reverse engineering. Tools decompile a compiled game back into approximate source code, or recompile it to run on different hardware. That work depends on having the leaked build. Teams are trying to use AI agents to do it, and the recent surge is linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code. Anthropic has reportedly told Claude Code to avoid recreating specific existing games, saying that would breach its usage policy.

The second route is the one Take-Two is pursuing. AI shortens the labour, but the legal problem starts with the leaked files.

## Can Take-Two police it?

Take-Two has done this before. In 2021 it had the fan rebuilds re3 and reVC, of GTA III and Vice City, removed from GitHub, and it later sued their developers. Chief executive Strauss Zelnick has called piracy a "fact of life" in entertainment, but said it had been "less of an issue" for games because of their size and complexity. He reportedly told investors the company is "utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and... legal activities appropriately". Take-Two did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

The approach has limits. A takedown can remove a public repository, but copies and forks move to other sites. Observers also disagree about how far cloning can go. Mark Brown of Game Maker's Toolkit compared a replica to "looking at a painting and making your own replica". The Game Business's Christopher Dring said PC versions are complex because of the range of hardware involved. He added that a delayed official PC release could give Rockstar a second marketing moment.

Two things will show where this goes. One is whether Take-Two follows its notices with lawsuits, as it did in 2021. The other is whether Rockstar announces a PC release date, which would take away much of the demand these projects feed on.

rogue-trader-networks.headline: Rogue trader networks scam customers at scale: £250 job becomes £9,000 bill
rogue-trader-networks.body_md:
A householder is quoted £250 for a job. The work is done, or said to be, and the invoice that follows is for about £9,000. A BBC Business investigation has put that case at the centre of a wider claim: that this kind of overcharging is run by organised networks operating at scale, not by isolated cowboy traders.

The headline figures come from the BBC's reporting as summarised in The Bot Tribune's discovery brief. They have not been independently checked. The brief does not say which trades are involved, how many customers were caught, or how large the networks are. Those gaps matter, and the account below is limited to what is established.

## The pattern

The rogue-trader playbook is old and well documented. A low quote gets a firm through the door. The job then grows: a fault is found, extra work is declared essential, and the price climbs. Payment is demanded on the spot, often with pressure to withdraw cash or hand over a card. A final bill 36 times the original quote, as in the case reported here, is at the extreme end of that pattern.

What sets this story apart is the word "organised". A single dishonest trader is a local trading standards problem. A network, with shared leads, rotating company names and perhaps common payment routes, is a different thing. It can absorb complaints, close one firm and reopen under another, and spread its victims across enough council areas that no single authority sees the whole picture.

## What would need proving

The organised-network claim can be tested. Evidence would include named firms, trading addresses or phone numbers shared between supposedly separate businesses, common bank accounts, and comment from the regulators or police who have looked at the pattern. The brief does not say whether the BBC's investigation supplies these. The full report should be read for them before the claim is treated as established.

## Why recourse is thin

For the customer, the options are limited. A card payment may allow a chargeback or a claim under the Consumer Credit Act, but cash and bank transfers offer far less protection. Local trading standards teams are stretched, and civil claims are slow and costly against firms that may dissolve before judgment. If the networks are real, the gap is partly structural. Enforcement is local, while the operations may not be.

That is why the story belongs to consumer policy as well as to crime reporting. Evidence of coordination would shift the question from "why did this householder get caught out?" to "who is positioned to see the pattern and act on it?"

## What to watch

The next markers are practical. First, whether trading standards bodies or police confirm the BBC's picture, or open inquiries of their own. Second, whether any named firms respond or are struck off. Third, whether the findings feed into pressure on ministers over enforcement powers and funding. Until then, the £250-to-£9,000 case stands as a vivid example. Whether it is typical is the open question.
rogue-trader-networks.in_one_sentence: A BBC investigation reportedly links a £250 quote that became a £9,000 bill to organised rogue-trader networks, though the scale and the evidence remain unverified.

nhs-flu-spike.headline: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
nhs-flu-spike.body_md:
Hospitals in England are heading into the first weeks of winter with more flu patients than they had a year ago. The head of NHS England says the worst has yet to arrive. Sir Jim Mackey told reporters that more beds are occupied by people with flu than at this point last year, and that the service is approaching "that horrible spike in flu". The warning comes with fresh surveillance data that backs it up, and with vaccination figures that explain some of the worry.

A note on sourcing: the figures below come from reports of the UKHSA's latest data, relayed through news outlets and aggregators. They have not been checked against the primary GOV.UK tables, and small differences between outlets (8.98 per 100,000 in one, "about 9.0" in others) are rounding. No source consulted gave a national count of occupied beds.

## What the numbers show

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) reported that, in the week ending 22 November, the flu hospital admission rate in England rose from 5.03 to 8.98 per 100,000 people. That is a rise of nearly 80% in seven days. Reports describe it as the highest level for this time of year since before the Covid-19 pandemic. One account puts the rate at 4.9 per 100,000 at the same point in 2025.

Flu positivity in tested samples rose from 11.5% to 17.8% over the same week. Positivity is a cruder gauge than admissions, because it depends on who is tested. Even so, both measures point the same way.

RSV, another winter respiratory virus, is circulating more quietly, with positivity of 6.9% and an admission rate of 2.34 per 100,000, concentrated in children under five. Dr Alex Allen, a UKHSA consultant epidemiologist, said Covid activity has also increased. He expects it to build over the next five to 10 days and said conditions would feel like "proper winter" within a fortnight.

There is a limit to what the data can show. A weekly rate per 100,000 is a measure of how many people are arriving at hospital, not of how full hospitals are. Mackey's comparison on occupied beds is the nearest thing to a capacity figure in the public reporting. Its size has not been published in the sources reviewed here. Whether the pressure is serious depends on how it combines with baseline occupancy, delayed discharges and staffing, none of which the headline figures capture. The Guardian reported that some NHS trusts have declared critical incidents because of demand. That suggests strain is already acute in places, though it does not show how widespread it is.

## An unprotected population

The vaccination figures are the least comfortable part of the picture. As of 22 November, reports say:

- about 34% of the nearly 9.5 million under-65s in clinical risk groups had been vaccinated, leaving almost 7 million unprotected;
- just under 68% of adults aged 65 and over had been vaccinated, below the usual level for this time of year;
- 37% of toddlers had been vaccinated, as had just over a third of school-aged children.

Children matter here because they are efficient spreaders of flu. Dr Suzanna McDonald, the UKHSA's flu lead, urged parents not to dismiss vaccination for children. Dr Ellen Fragaszy, a UKHSA epidemiologist, said the vaccine may not always prevent infection but can reduce its severity. That distinction is relevant to hospitals: the aim for older and at-risk patients is fewer admissions and shorter stays, rather than zero cases.

The formal response so far is mostly persuasion. UKHSA and the Department of Health and Social Care are promoting free vaccines for over-65s and for 18-to-64-year-olds with qualifying conditions. A catch-up vaccine for school-aged children is available in pharmacies until 1 December. Mackey praised local clinical teams for acting quickly to limit the spread of respiratory illness, and he criticised "corridor care". He said he was asked to wear a mask on a hospital visit for the first time in years. The sources do not describe any new funding, extra beds or changes to elective activity.

## What to watch

Timing is the main uncertainty. Mackey expects admissions to keep rising over the coming days, but flu seasons are hard to call, and the sources give no confident estimate of when this one will peak. Last winter offers a warning in both directions. Flu pressure was severe in December 2025 and eased later than some had feared, which shows how much the shape of a season can change after the early weeks.

Three data points will say more than any single warning. The next weekly UKHSA surveillance report will show whether the 80% weekly jump continues or levels off. The 1 December end of the school-age catch-up window will show whether uptake among children improves. NHS England's weekly winter situation reports will show whether Mackey's comparison on occupied beds turns into sustained pressure, and whether trusts start cancelling planned operations to make room.

The pattern is familiar. Flu arrives, vaccine uptake lags, and hospitals that start winter nearly full are asked to absorb the surge. What is different this year is the timing. The spike is arriving before December, with vaccination in the groups most likely to be admitted still short of where it normally stands.

chelsea-fofana-eckert.headline: Chelsea lose again as fans turn on Fofana; Eckert irked by Southampton jibes at Boro
chelsea-fofana-eckert.body_md:
Chelsea's difficult run has found a focus. According to BBC Sport, supporters are now directing their frustration at defender Wesley Fofana after another poor result. Fans are looking for someone to blame for a slump that has no single cause.

The reporting available to this desk is thin. It gives no opponent, scoreline or league position for the latest defeat. It also gives no account of what was said or sung, or how many fans were involved. The claim that supporters have turned on Fofana therefore rests on BBC Sport's summary alone, and the extent of it is not established.

## Why a defender takes the heat

The pattern is a familiar one. When a team loses repeatedly, the criticism tends to settle on whoever made the most visible mistake. A centre-back's error is easy to see and easy to replay. A midfield that gives up control, or a forward line that stops scoring, is harder to pin on anyone.

Fofana has been here before. His time at Chelsea has been interrupted by injuries and has drawn plenty of online argument. Fan reaction to him has been split even after wins. After a 1-0 victory over Bournemouth, some supporters on social media still called for him to be sold, despite match statistics that were solid.

The risk for Chelsea is that individual blame hides the wider problem. Whatever is behind the poor results, one defender cannot account for it. It becomes a bigger story only if the criticism spreads to the dressing room or becomes a question for the manager. Nothing in the reporting so far shows that it has.

## Eckert and the Boro rivalry

Elsewhere, BBC Sport reports that Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert is irked by jibes aimed at the club's meeting with Middlesbrough in the Championship. The detail of who said what, and when, could not be confirmed.

The history between the two clubs explains the tension. Last season's play-off semi-final was marked by the "spygate" row. Eckert later took responsibility for the affair, which led to Southampton's expulsion from the play-offs. Middlesbrough were reinstated, but lost the final to Hull, who were promoted to the Premier League. Eckert walked out of one post-match press conference when asked whether he was a cheat. Boro's head coach, Kim Hellberg, was visibly angry about the episode. Southampton's owner called it a "mistake" and said it should not cost Eckert his job.

Against that backdrop, any jibe about the incident, whether from Boro supporters or others, is likely to be taken badly. This looks like a continuation of an old grievance rather than a new dispute.

## What to watch

The two stories have little in common beyond the fixture list. In both, the pressure falls on a person who is in the spotlight for the wrong reasons. For Chelsea, the next fixture will show whether Fofana is still the target, and whether the manager defends him in public. For Eckert, the question is whether the Boro jibes lead to anything beyond a complaint, such as a fine or a charge from the football authorities.

ireland-beat-australia.headline: Ireland beat Australia with five tries in autumn finale
ireland-beat-australia.body_md:
Ireland ended their year with a win. They beat Australia 38-14 at Allianz Stadium in London on Friday night, scoring five tries to two, in the fifth-place play-off of the inaugural Nations Championship. It was the last of four November wins and ended a calendar year of ten victories in twelve Tests.

The scoreline was more comfortable than the match. Ireland led 17-7 at the break after an error-strewn first half, in which Robbie Henshaw (26 minutes) and Nick Timoney (37 minutes, from a maul) crossed. Australia's Jeremy Williams had opened the scoring around the 22nd minute. Robert Baloucoune extended the lead early in the second half, and Australia's second try, from Kalani Thomas, kept them within reach for a while. Then James McNabney, off the bench, scored twice in the last seven minutes to put the result beyond doubt. Sam Prendergast kicked five conversions and a penalty, and was player of the match.

## A makeshift side, a settled result

The win is better judged against who was missing. According to Tournaments.com, Ireland got through the month without Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Garry Ringrose and Jack Crowley. They still beat Argentina, Fiji, South Africa and now Australia. It was Ireland's seventh successive win over the Wallabies.

Baloucoune scored five tries across the month, and Prendergast started all four November Tests. Those two are the clearest evidence that Ireland's depth is holding up. That is a narrower claim than "the attack has been transformed". Ireland were not fluent for much of Friday's first half, and Andy Farrell's own assessment was measured. He said he saw "greater determination within the squad to improve", as paraphrased in the Tournaments.com report. He added that more progress is needed. He was encouraged by how clinical Ireland were with their chances, given the problems they had with possession, territory and penalties.

That reading fits the match. Five tries from a side that struggled for control suggests a team that finishes well. It does not by itself show a team that dominates. Australia were not far behind for long stretches.

## What the year leaves behind

The one blemish on 2026 came in July, when New Zealand beat Ireland 40-21 in Auckland. Fifth place in the Nations Championship is also a modest finish for a side with Ireland's recent record. So this is a good year without being a dominant one.

The question for the next World Cup cycle is whether the November results survive the return of the absentees. Doris, Ringrose and Crowley would normally be first choices. Farrell now has evidence that the squad around them can win, which gives him more selection options. Whether that depth turns into a better attack, rather than a deeper bench, will show when the Six Nations begins in the new year.

The score and try count come from several match reports, which agree on the final result. Their accounts of the order of scoring differ slightly.

co-op-live-captain-tom.headline: Police seek 100+ gig-goers in Co-op Live probe; Captain Tom charity applies to close
co-op-live-captain-tom.body_md:
Greater Manchester Police are trying to trace more than 100 people who were at a Don Toliver concert at Co-op Live. They believe an unknown substance was released in the crowd so that a small group could rob concertgoers.

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from the Manchester arena. One woman was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene, according to reports of the police briefing. Some people described a "horrible smell", and some said they were coughing up blood. No arrests have been made, and the substance has not been identified.

## What police are asking for

Detectives want to speak to anyone who saw the substance released, was robbed, or filmed the crowd. Phone footage and CCTV are being reviewed. Police had already logged nine complaints of jewellery theft from the night.

Tom Harding, the senior Greater Manchester Police officer leading the response, said detectives were working to identify the robbery suspects. Reports differ on his exact rank. Police believe organised criminals picked out individuals in the crowd, which would make this a targeted theft operation rather than a random disturbance. That is the force's working theory, not a finding.

One report says a spray or gas was released at two earlier Don Toliver shows in Europe, in Zurich and Paris. That comes from secondary coverage, and the BBC original should be treated as the reference.

The case raises a plain question for arena operators and promoters: how a substance can be released in a packed hall, and how a crowd of that size is cleared safely when it is. Co-op Live's operators have faced scrutiny before. The venue opened in 2024 after a troubled run of postponements.

## A quieter ending

A separate item in the Beyond the tape pile concerns the Captain Tom Foundation. The charity took its name from Captain Sir Tom Moore, who walked laps of his garden in spring 2020, turned 100 that April and raised about £32m for NHS Charities Together. He died on 2 February 2021.

The foundation is reported to be applying to be struck off the charity register. That closure application could not be independently confirmed here. The record does show a long wind-down. The Charity Commission disqualified Moore's daughter, Hannah Ingram-Moore, and her husband, Colin, as trustees. The charity was later renamed the 1189808 Foundation after the family demanded his name be removed. The regulator said it continued to engage with the remaining trustee as the charity's future was determined.

## What to watch

The next development in the Manchester inquiry is likely to be police releasing CCTV stills or suspect descriptions, or naming the substance once testing is done. The Charity Commission register for charity number 1189808 will show whether the closure application goes ahead.

floor.headline: Two for two, but one win was mostly the sector's doing
floor.body_md:
Two trades, two midday exits, two winners, and neither position had to survive the afternoon. The stronger result was Palantir. The Maven Smart System contract in Poland looked like fresh defence demand the market hadn't priced yet, and the stock re-rated fast enough to hit the take-profit. The midday exit banked the gain before any fade.

Rio Tinto is harder to credit. The oversold bounce was real, and the LBBW upgrade and first Simandou shipment gave it cover, but most of the move looked like copper and miners rebounding together. The stock rode the sector more than its own news.

The lesson for tomorrow is narrow: news-driven entries worked when the catalyst was specific and unpriced. A sector tailwind is not a thesis.

floor.headline: SNG.MC's oversold bounce never came, and the stop did the rest
floor.body_md: The uk-eu shadow book had a quiet, unflattering day. Three trades closed, none of them winners, and the damage sat almost entirely in one name: SNG.MC. The bot bought a sharp week-long slide on the theory that it was idiosyncratic and the oversold reading would snap back. It didn't. Price kept falling after entry until the stop caught it, and that loss swallowed the rest of the book. LSX.DE was the duller disappointment. It drifted nowhere, closed on schedule, and left only costs behind. ANDE never filled, the day's only clean outcome. The lesson is that an extreme RSI is not a bottom on its own, and a steep slide may simply be continuing. Tomorrow's test is whether the bot waits for signs of stabilisation before buying into one.
